title: Remove a keystone predator: sea otters and kelp forests

stimulus.title: Part of a kelp forest food web
stimulus.html: Along rocky Pacific coasts, giant kelp (a large brown alga) grows in underwater forests. Sea urchins graze on kelp, and sea otters eat sea urchins. Many fish species shelter, feed and lay eggs among the kelp. In the 1990s, the sea otter population of one island chain fell by about 90% within a decade; the leading explanation is that killer whales there began eating far more otters than before.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Sea otters are a keystone species in this community. Describe what makes a species a keystone species.

rubric.point: Describes a species whose effect on community structure is much larger than its abundance (or biomass) would suggest; its removal causes large changes in the community.
accept: a species with a disproportionately large effect relative to its numbers
removing it changes the whole community, even though it is not abundant
its role, not its biomass, holds the community structure together

parts.sample: A keystone species has an effect on its community far larger than its numbers or biomass would suggest. Sea otters are not very abundant, but when they are removed, the structure of the whole kelp forest community changes.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the decline in sea otters is likely to affect the amount of kelp.

rubric.point: Explains a trophic cascade: fewer otters means fewer urchins are eaten, so the urchin population grows; more urchins graze more kelp, so the amount of kelp decreases.
accept: fewer otters, more urchins, less kelp
urchins are released from predation and overgraze the kelp
a trophic cascade: removing the top predator lets the herbivore increase and the producer decrease

parts.sample: With fewer otters eating them, more sea urchins survive and the urchin population grows. The larger urchin population grazes kelp faster than it can regrow, so the kelp forest shrinks. This is a trophic cascade passing from the otters down to the producers.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict how the number of kelp-forest fish species will change over the next decade, and justify your prediction.

rubric.point: Predicts a decrease in kelp-forest fish species (and in their numbers), because kelp, a foundation species, provides their shelter, egg-laying sites and food; as kelp is lost, so is their habitat.
accept: fewer fish species, because their kelp habitat disappears
decrease, since the fish depend on kelp for shelter and food
fish species decline as urchins turn kelp forest into bare rock

parts.sample: The number of kelp-forest fish species will decrease. These fish depend on kelp for shelter, egg-laying sites and food. As urchins graze the kelp away, that habitat disappears, so species that need it decline or vanish from the area.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: An ecologist claims that a decline of 90% in one species of kelp-forest fish would change the community much less than the 90% decline in sea otters did. Justify this claim.

rubric.point: Justifies that the fish species is one of many with similar roles (other fish fill its role), and it does not control a strong consumer of the habitat, whereas otters control urchins, so their loss cascades through the food web and removes the kelp habitat.
accept: other fish species do similar jobs and can compensate, but nothing replaces the otters' control of urchins
the fish is not a keystone species; its loss does not set off a trophic cascade
otters regulate urchins, which control kelp, so their loss affects every level; the fish's loss does not

parts.sample: The fish is one of many fish species that eat similar food in the kelp forest, so others can take over its role, and it does not control any species that shapes the habitat. Sea otters are the main predator of urchins: their loss lets urchins destroy the kelp, which removes the habitat for many species. So the otter decline sets off a cascade through the whole community, while the fish decline mainly affects that one species.
